title: Makkah Pact Allies Hold Emergency Riyadh Talks as Houthi Attacks Escalate
excerpt: The Makkah Joint Defence Agreement's political and defence committee will meet in Riyadh next week to decide next steps on Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, while Iran has proposed a political track as an alternative to military action.
body:
• Pakistan's Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar announced on October 2 that the strategic political and defence committee of the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement will hold an emergency meeting in Riyadh next week to decide next steps on escalating Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia.
  • The three-member pact — Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan — signed on August 7 treats an armed attack on any one member as an attack on all three; the three countries' military chiefs met in Riyadh on September 25 and condemned the Houthi attacks.
  • Dar said Iran has suggested engaging Yemen's Houthis politically as an alternative to "kinetic action," and that Tehran has distanced itself from the Houthis and Iraqi militias.
  • Saudi air defences intercepted six Houthi ballistic missiles aimed at Taif and Yanbu this week, and a Houthi drone was destroyed south of Mecca before it could enter restricted airspace over the holy city.

Emergency meeting in Riyadh

Pakistan's Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said on Friday that an emergency meeting of the strategic political and defence committee under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement will be held in Riyadh next week to decide the alliance's next steps on Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia. Speaking at a news conference in Islamabad, Dar said the exact date would be confirmed later and that whatever course of action is decided would be shared publicly after the meeting.

Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan are the pact's three members. Dar said more than six other countries are keen to join the agreement, but new membership requests cannot be entertained until the pact is fully operational — a process he said could take up to a year.

The Makkah pact and the Houthi threat

The three countries signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement on August 7, pledging to treat an armed attack on any one of them as an attack on all three, while providing for broader defence cooperation. The pact is the alliance's first formal collective-defence test.

The meeting was called after the three countries' foreign ministers — Saudi Arabia's Prince Faisal bin Farhan, Pakistan's Ishaq Dar and Turkey's Hakan Fidan — met in New York and discussed the escalating attacks and implementation of the pact. On September 25, the three countries' military chiefs met in Riyadh and "strongly condemned the attacks on Makkah and on the Kingdom's civil and economic infrastructure," agreeing to advance intelligence cooperation, military coordination and integration of defence capabilities.

Pakistan's Defence Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif has said Islamabad stands unequivocally behind the kingdom under the agreement, pledging to defend Saudi Arabia by "whatever means" are required — though he did not say whether Pakistan had joined Saudi strikes against the Houthis or received a request for direct military assistance. No joint combat deployment or specific operational measures have been announced.

"There is no written, solid offer. It is brainstorming between two foreign ministers."

— Ishaq Dar, Pakistan's Foreign Minister

Dar revealed that Iran had suggested a political approach to engaging the Houthis — a suggestion he said was made in good faith and would be discussed at the Riyadh meeting as an alternative to "kinetic action." He said Iran had distanced itself from the Houthis and Iraqi militias, and that President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi both wanted the matter concluded.

Saudi Arabia has accused the Houthis of targeting Islam's two holiest cities. This week, Saudi civil defence activated the kingdom's National Early Warning Platform, issuing alerts for Mecca, Jeddah, Taif, Yanbu and Tabuk amid a potential missile or drone threat; authorities later gave the all-clear. Saudi-led coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki said six ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis were intercepted and destroyed before they could strike Taif and the Red Sea industrial city of Yanbu. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree separately claimed the group had launched dozens of ballistic missiles and drones against Saudi military positions, including targets in the Jazan region — claims that were not independently confirmed.

Regional security and energy stakes

The escalation has placed fresh pressure on energy infrastructure and shipping at a moment when the wider Middle East is already disrupted. The UN Security Council has been told that Yemen has returned to large-scale fighting after the relative calm that followed the 2022 truce, with Houthi operations expanding across several fronts, including attacks on civilian and energy infrastructure inside Saudi Arabia, and displacement rising sharply inside Yemen.

The Arabian Post reported that Saudi Arabia has leaned on routes designed to reduce its exposure to the Strait of Hormuz, which Dar described as a central bargaining chip in efforts to end the nearly seven-month US-Iran conflict. Dar said there should be no fee or charges to cross the blockaded strait. The fighting has also sharpened focus on the Bab el-Mandeb, the narrow passage connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden, with UN officials warning that threats to commercial vessels could endanger freedom of navigation along a route central to global trade.

Inside the kingdom, Saudi Arabia's Grand Mufti, Sheikh Saleh bin Fawzan Al-Fawzan, issued an unusually forceful message to troops stationed on the kingdom's frontiers, urging them to remain prepared, describing the defeat of the Houthis and those supporting them as among the greatest duties.

What it means for Indians in the Gulf

Millions of Indians live and work across Saudi Arabia and the Gulf, including large communities in Jeddah, Taif and Yanbu — cities that were directly named in this week's missile alerts and interception announcements. The alert for Mecca also reaches the thousands of Indian pilgrims who travel annually for Hajj and Umrah, as Saudi authorities have accused the Houthis of targeting Islam's two holiest cities. Any sustained escalation would put pressure on aviation routes, travel plans and energy prices that feed directly into remittance-dependent households in India.

What to watch

The immediate focus is the Riyadh meeting itself: the exact date has not been announced, and Dar said the alliance's decided course of action will be shared publicly afterward. Key questions include whether the three members commit to joint operational measures beyond the intelligence-sharing and coordination already agreed in September, and whether the Iranian proposal for a political track gains traction inside the committee. Longer term, the pact's credibility as a collective-defence arrangement will be measured by what it does — not what it says — if Houthi attacks continue. Also on watch: whether any of the six-plus countries interested in joining are named, and how a second front in the Gulf affects efforts to end the US-Iran conflict.
